newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean labour minister to retain his post.
newsitem.headline: South Korean labour minister to retain his post.

text.p: South Korea's labour minister on Wednesday withdrew his resignation after President Kim Young-sam asked him to retain his post, a presidential Blue House official said.
Minister Jin Nyum offered to resign on Tuesday to take responsibility for a bungled effort to revise the labour law.
"President Kim Young-sam called Jin Nyum and asked him not to resign, and Minister Jin agreed to continue in his post," the official, who declined to be identified, told Reuters.
Jin's resignation offer came as a surprise since he survived a sweeping cabinet reshuffle earlier this month.
He strongly supported the introduction of clauses making it easier for companies to lay off workers and introducing flexible working hours in the first revision to the labour law.
That version, rammed through parliament last December, sparked weeks of wildcat strikes across South Korea in January.
Layoffs have been all but impossible in South Korea, where redundancies must be approved by a court.

The South Korean parliament passed a watered-down labour bill on March 10 after President Kim Young-sam was forced to send the law back for more debate. The new revision delays for two years implementation of the clause on layoffs.
A labour ministry spokesman said Jin cited his health and the need to take responsibility for touching off worker anger in January as reasons for his resignation offer.
He said Jin may have to have cataract surgery soon.
"Minister Jin said the new law must be implemented under a new minister," he added.
President Kim had earlier insisted a flexible labour market was essential to improve the country's industrial competitiveness and reduce a ballooning trade deficit.
The ruling New Korea Party also caved in to pressure from home and abroad by agreeing in the revised legislation to instantly recognise the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions.

Under the revised labour bill passed in March, multiple trade unions would be allowed at a national level immediately and at the company level by 2002. It would also require the abolition of wages for full-time union officials in five years.
It abandoned clauses allowing firms to sub-contract production and hire outside workers during strikes. The bill also says companies do not have to pay workers who walk out.
Jin was appointed labour minister in May 1995.
